reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: db.flush() with nothing marked and nobody subscribed
reading.floor: a call that bumps a frame counter
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR HERE IS ESSENTIALLY ZERO AND THE RATIO IS THEREFORE NOT A READING — take the absolute nanoseconds on our side and ignore the multiple. A hand-written store has no frame to close, so the nearest thing to a floor is the bookkeeping a person writes instead, and V8 inlines that to almost nothing. What ours does for the money: runs the effect graph's drain, swaps the two delivery lists, walks an empty delivery, runs the after-flush and after-each-frame phases, sweeps identities nobody holds and reports errors. This number is the fixed cost every other frame row carries, which is what makes it worth printing even though its ratio means nothing.

reading.ours: update the row, flush, and the subscription fires — per identity delivered
reading.floor: store the field and call the handler — per row
reading.caveat: ONE WRITE PER IDENTITY PER FRAME, WHICH IS THE WORST CASE FOR US. Both sides call the handler exactly once per row, so nothing here is saved by coalescing — the mechanism ours pays for on every write is deliberately given nothing to do. Ours per operation: the whole update path, then the stamp, then a push onto the frame's pending list, then the frame walking that list and asking the subscriber store to deliver. The floor: one store and one call. The fixed cost of the frame itself is divided by a thousand deliveries here; `flush.empty-vs-noop` prices it directly so a reader can subtract it. What ours buys and the floor cannot: the handler is registered against the identity, so a writer does not have to know who is listening.

reading.ours: db.subscribeToField(slot, 'title', h) — the narrowest signal the engine has
reading.floor: store the field and call h only when the name that moved is 'title'
reading.caveat: THE ONE COLUMN THAT MOVED IS THE ONE SUBSCRIBED TO, on both sides, so this is the happy case. Ours pays for it twice over: the write now RECORDS which columns moved (a per-identity list it would not otherwise keep — see the `movedFields` machinery), and the handler consults that list on delivery. The floor tests a string it already has. NOT PRICED HERE, and worth knowing before quoting this row: a field subscription is an ordinary subscription that filters, so two field subscriptions on one identity both wake and one returns having found its name absent — a write to `note` costs a `title` subscriber a frame and a delivery to discover it had nothing to show, where the floor's guard would not have been reached at all.

reading.ours: db.computed over one row, invalidated by a write and recomputed at the frame
reading.floor: set a dirty flag on write, recompute on read if dirty
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR IS A REAL MEMO AND DOES THE SAME JOB: it is invalidated by the write, it recomputes once however many writes landed, and it answers the same number. Two things it does not do. It recomputes LAZILY, at the read, where ours recomputes eagerly during the frame — so a value nobody reads is free for the floor and paid for by us. And it has no graph: a memo over another memo has to be invalidated by hand and in the right order, which is the whole of what `db.computed` is buying and is not exercised by a one-level derivation. Direction: inflates our ratio, and a deeper graph would move it back the other way by an amount this row cannot show. Ours additionally gates on equality before marking anything downstream, and the derivation here always changes, so that gate never saves us a wake-up.
